source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\01. Patents Act 1970 - Non-Patentable Inventions (Sec 3).docx
text: Context Section 3 of the Patents Act, 1970 lists categories that are excluded from the definition of a patentable 'invention'. The clauses below are the ones most relevant to biotechnology, pharmaceuticals and traditional-knowledge-based inventions.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\01. Patents Act 1970 - Non-Patentable Inventions (Sec 3).docx
text: Section 3(c) - Discoveries excluded The mere discovery of a scientific principle or the formulation of an abstract theory is not patentable. Amendment (post-TRIPS, 2002/2005): also excludes the mere discovery of any living thing or non-living substance occurring in nature (e.g. isolating a naturally occurring microorganism or gene is not, by itself, an invention).

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\01. Patents Act 1970 - Non-Patentable Inventions (Sec 3).docx
text: Section 3(d) - The 'known substance' / evergreening bar Excludes from patentability: The mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance. The mere discovery of any new property or new use for a known substance. The mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus, unless such known process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant. Significance: Section 3(d) is India's key anti-'evergreening' provision, aimed at stopping pharmaceutical companies from getting fresh patents on trivial modifications (new salts, polymorphs, isomers) of already-known drugs without a genuine efficacy improvement. It was famously upheld by the Supreme Court in Novartis AG v. Union of India (2013), which denied a patent on Glivec (imatinib mesylate).

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\01. Patents Act 1970 - Non-Patentable Inventions (Sec 3).docx
text: Section 3(p) - Traditional knowledge bar An invention which, in effect, is traditional knowledge, or which is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of a traditionally known component or components, is not patentable. Significance: This clause is the direct statutory hook used (along with TKDL prior-art evidence) to oppose or revoke patents claiming known Ayurvedic/traditional formulations or uses (e.g. the turmeric wound-healing and basmati rice cases).

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\01. Patents Act 1970 - Non-Patentable Inventions (Sec 3).docx
text: Quick recap for exams 3(c): discoveries of natural things/principles → not inventions. 3(d): new form/new use/new property of a known substance without enhanced efficacy → not patentable (anti-evergreening). 3(p): traditional knowledge or mere aggregation of known TK properties → not patentable. Note: Source excerpt covers Section 3(c), 3(d) and 3(p) only; see file 02 for the full Act.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\02. Patents Act 1970 - Full Act Overview.docx
text: What it is The primary Indian statute governing the grant, administration, working and enforcement of patents. Enacted in 1970 (replacing the 1911 Act), it has been amended several times (notably 1999, 2002, 2005 for TRIPS compliance) and its Rules were most recently amended in 2024.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\02. Patents Act 1970 - Full Act Overview.docx
text: Chapter map (23 chapters) I - Preliminary (Ss. 1-2): title, extent, commencement, definitions. II - Inventions not patentable (Ss. 3-4): Sec. 3 exclusions (see file 01) and atomic-energy inventions. III - Applications for patents (Ss. 6-11): who may apply, form, foreign-filing disclosure, provisional/complete specification, priority date. IV - Publication and examination (Ss. 11A-15): 18-month publication, request for examination (within 48 months), examiner's report, Controller's powers. V - Opposition proceedings (Ss. 25-28): pre-grant opposition (Sec. 25(1)) and post-grant opposition (Sec. 25(2)). VI - Anticipation (Ss. 29-34): what does/does not destroy novelty (prior publication, prior use, public display, government communication). VII - Secrecy provisions (Ss. 35-42): defence-related inventions. VIII - Grant of patents and rights conferred (Ss. 43-53): term of patent = 20 years from filing date (Sec. 53); rights of patentee (Sec. 48). IX - Patents of addition (Ss. 54-56). X - Amendment of applications/specifications (Ss. 57-59). XI - Restoration of lapsed patents (Ss. 60-62). XII - Surrender and revocation of patents (Ss. 63-66). XIII - Register of Patents (Ss. 67-72). XIV - Patent Office and establishment (Ss. 73-75): Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks; Patent Offices (Kolkata HQ + Chennai, Mumbai, Delhi branches). XV - Powers of Controller generally (Ss. 77-78). XVI - Working of patents, compulsory licences, revocation (Ss. 82-94): compulsory licence grounds - reasonable requirements of the public not satisfied, invention not worked in India, not available at reasonably affordable price (Sec. 84); can be applied for after 3 years from grant. XVII - Government use and acquisition of inventions (Ss. 99-103). XVIII - Suits for infringement (Ss. 104-115): jurisdiction, reliefs (injunction, damages/account of profits), defences. XIX - Appeals (Ss. 116-117A): to the High Court (post the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, which abolished the IPAB). XX - Penalties (Ss. 118-124). XXI - Patent agents (Ss. 125-132): qualifications, register of patent agents. XXII - International arrangements (Ss. 133-140): PCT applications, convention countries. XXIII - Miscellaneous (Ss. 141-162): includes Sec. 146 (working statements), delegation, rule-making power.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\02. Patents Act 1970 - Full Act Overview.docx
text: Key concepts to remember Patentability criteria: novelty, inventive step (non-obviousness), industrial applicability + not falling within Sec. 3/4 exclusions. Term of every patent: 20 years from the date of filing (uniform for all types since 2002 amendment). Pre-grant opposition: any person; Post-grant opposition: only a 'person interested', within 1 year of grant. Compulsory licensing (Sec. 84-92): India's best-known invocation was the 2012 Natco v. Bayer (Nexavar) compulsory licence. Patents (Amendment) Rules, 2024 - headline changes Introduced a certificate of inventorship, streamlined pre-grant opposition timelines, extended the request-for-examination window flexibility, eased the filing of divisional applications, and reduced the frequency/burden of Form 27 (working statement) filings. Note: Source: full consolidated text of the Act (23 chapters).

source_title: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration & Protection) Act, 1999
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\03. Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999.docx
text: Purpose Provides for the registration and better protection of geographical indications (GIs) relating to goods in India, in compliance with India's TRIPS obligations (Articles 22-24). Administered by the Geographical Indications Registry, Chennai.

source_title: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration & Protection) Act, 1999
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\03. Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999.docx
text: Key definitions (Section 2) Geographical Indication: an indication identifying goods as originating in a region/locality of India, where a given quality, reputation or characteristic is essentially attributable to that geographical origin (covers agricultural, natural or manufactured goods, incl. foodstuffs, handicrafts, industrial goods). Authorised user: a person registered as an authorised user under Section 17, entitled to use the registered GI. Deceptively similar: a GI is deceptively similar to another if it so nearly resembles it as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion. Registered proprietor: any association of persons, producers, or organisation representing the interest of the producers of the goods (individuals generally cannot register a GI in their own name).

source_title: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration & Protection) Act, 1999
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\03. Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999.docx
text: Registration scheme Application filed with the Registrar of Geographical Indications, Chennai; examined, published in the GI Journal, subject to opposition, then registered. Initial protection: 10 years, renewable indefinitely for further periods of 10 years. GIs cannot be assigned, transmitted, licensed, pledged or mortgaged (unlike trademarks) - they belong to the community/producers of that region.

source_title: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration & Protection) Act, 1999
section_or_article: Overview - Relevance to traditional knowledge / Ayurveda
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\03. Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999.docx
text: Relevance to traditional knowledge / Ayurveda GI protection is one of the sui generis IP tools (alongside TKDL and Sec. 3(p) of the Patents Act) used to protect India's traditional products - e.g. Darjeeling Tea, Basmati Rice, Kancheepuram Silk, and various Ayurvedic/herbal products tied to a specific region, from misappropriation and misuse of the geographical name. Note: Source excerpt: Section 2 definitions.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\04. Trade Marks Act, 1999.docx
text: Purpose Governs registration and protection of trademarks in India; replaced the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958, to align with TRIPS. Administered by the Registrar of Trade Marks under the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM).

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\04. Trade Marks Act, 1999.docx
text: Key definitions (Section 2) Trade mark: a mark capable of being represented graphically and capable of distinguishing the goods/services of one person from those of others; may include shape of goods, packaging and combination of colours. Mark: includes a device, brand, heading, label, ticket, name, signature, word, letter, numeral, shape of goods, packaging or combination of colours. Controller: the Controller-General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (Sec. 3). 'Article' and 'well-known trade mark', 'certification trade mark', 'collective mark' are also defined for their special registration categories.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\04. Trade Marks Act, 1999.docx
text: Key scheme points Registration is valid for 10 years, renewable indefinitely for successive 10-year terms. Goods/services classified per the NICE Classification (45 classes). Both registered and unregistered marks are protectable - infringement action for registered marks, passing-off action for unregistered marks.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\04. Trade Marks Act, 1999.docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme Trademarks (and certification marks) can be used to protect brand names associated with Ayurvedic/herbal products and Ayush certification marks, complementing GI and patent-based protection of traditional knowledge. Note: Source excerpt: Section 2 definitions.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\05. Designs Act, 2000.docx
text: Purpose Protects the visual/aesthetic features (shape, configuration, pattern, ornament, composition of lines/colours) applied to an article, which appeal to and are judged solely by the eye. Replaced the Designs Act, 1911; TRIPS-compliant.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\05. Designs Act, 2000.docx
text: Key definitions (Section 2) Article: any article of manufacture, including any part of an article capable of being made and sold separately (same wording as the Trade Marks Act). Design: features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines/colours applied to an article by any industrial process, judged solely by the eye - excludes any mode or principle of construction, or anything that is purely functional. Controller: Controller-General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\05. Designs Act, 2000.docx
text: Key scheme points A design must be new/original and not previously published/used to be registrable. Registration confers copyright (as statutorily defined - exclusive right to apply the design) for an initial 10 years, extendable once by 5 years. Registered designs are distinct from and cannot overlap with 'artistic works' under the Copyright Act once industrially applied more than 50 times.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\05. Designs Act, 2000.docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme Design protection can cover distinctive packaging or ornamentation used for traditional/Ayurvedic product lines, though it does not protect traditional patterns/motifs that are already in the public domain (prior publication bar). Note: Source excerpt: Section 2 definitions.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\06. Copyright Act, 1957.docx
text: Purpose Protects original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, cinematograph films and sound recordings. Grants the author a bundle of exclusive economic and moral rights.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\06. Copyright Act, 1957.docx
text: Key definitions (Section 2) Adaptation: conversion of a work from one form to another - e.g. a dramatic work into a non-dramatic work, or a literary/artistic work into a dramatic work by way of performance, or abridgement/alteration/re-arrangement of the work. (Section 2 also defines: 'artistic work', 'author', 'broadcast', 'copyright', 'cinematograph film', 'literary work', 'performer', 'sound recording', 'work of joint authorship', etc. - the full list runs through most of the alphabet and underpins every substantive provision of the Act.)

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\06. Copyright Act, 1957.docx
text: Key scheme points Copyright subsists automatically on creation and fixation - no registration is mandatory (though the Copyright Office register is useful evidence). Duration: generally life of the author + 60 years (for literary/dramatic/musical/artistic works); 60 years from publication for films, sound recordings, and works of corporate/anonymous authorship. Exclusive rights include reproduction, issue of copies, public performance, communication to the public, adaptation and translation; moral rights (Sec. 57) - right of paternity and integrity - survive even after assignment of economic rights. Fair dealing exceptions exist under Section 52 (research, private use, criticism/review, reporting current events, educational use, etc.).

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\06. Copyright Act, 1957.docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme Copyright does not protect traditional knowledge itself (which lacks a single identifiable 'author' and is often ancient/in the public domain), but can protect original compilations, databases (e.g. TKDL's classification and translation work) and derivative commentaries on traditional texts. Note: Source excerpt: Section 2 definitions.

source_title: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights (PPV&FR) Act, 2001
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\07. Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers Rights Act, 2001.docx
text: Purpose India's sui generis (non-patent) legislation for plant variety protection, mandated by TRIPS Article 27.3(b). Uniquely among such laws worldwide, it gives farmers rights on par with formal plant breeders. Administered by the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority (PPV&FRA).

source_title: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights (PPV&FR) Act, 2001
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\07. Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers Rights Act, 2001.docx
text: Section 39 - Farmers' Rights (core provisions) A farmer who has bred or developed a new variety is entitled to registration and protection in like manner as a breeder under the Act. A 'farmers' variety' is entitled to registration if the application contains the declarations specified under Sec. 18(1)(h). Farmers are entitled to save, use, sow, re-sow, exchange, share or sell their farm produce of a protected variety, including seed - EXCEPT they cannot sell branded seed of a protected variety. Farmers are also recognised/rewarded for conservation of plant genetic resources through the Plant Genome Savior Community/individual recognition/award, and for contributing to the national gene bank. Farmers are exempted from paying any fee in any proceeding before the Authority/Registrar/Tribunal/High Court under the Act.

source_title: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights (PPV&FR) Act, 2001
section_or_article: Overview - Other structural points to know
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\07. Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers Rights Act, 2001.docx
text: Other structural points to know Grants Plant Breeders' Rights (PBR) for new, distinct, uniform and stable (DUS) varieties, and also allows registration of extant varieties (already in commercial use). Term of protection: 18 years for trees/vines; 15 years for other crops; 9 years for extant varieties (renewable up to those maxima). Establishes benefit-sharing: any person can claim benefit sharing from a registered variety's commercial use if it draws on their genetic material/traditional knowledge.

source_title: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights (PPV&FR) Act, 2001
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\07. Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers Rights Act, 2001.docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme The Act balances formal plant-breeders' IP rights with farmers' customary rights to seed and recognises the contribution of traditional/indigenous farming communities to crop genetic diversity - directly linking to CBD/Nagoya benefit-sharing principles. Note: Source excerpt: Section 39 (Farmers' Rights).

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\08. Biological Diversity Act, 2002.docx
text: Purpose India's domestic legislation implementing the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) - provides for conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from the use of biological resources and associated traditional knowledge.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\08. Biological Diversity Act, 2002.docx
text: Key definitions (Section 2) Access: collecting, procuring or possessing any biological resource occurring in/obtained from India, or associated traditional knowledge, for research, bio-survey or commercial utilisation. Benefit claimers: conservers of biological resources, their by-products, creators and holders of knowledge/information relating to the use of such biological resources, innovations and practices associated with such use.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\08. Biological Diversity Act, 2002.docx
text: Three-tier institutional structure National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) - regulates access by foreign entities/non-resident Indians; approves grant of IPR based on Indian biological material. State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) - regulate access by Indian citizens/entities at the state level. Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) - at local/panchayat level; maintain People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs).

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\08. Biological Diversity Act, 2002.docx
text: Key operative provisions Prior approval of the NBA is required before applying for any IPR (in India or abroad) based on research/information from biological resources obtained from India. Foreign nationals/companies/NRIs need prior NBA approval to access Indian biological resources for research or commercial use; Indian citizens/entities generally need only intimate the SBB. The NBA determines benefit-sharing terms - can include monetary compensation, joint IPR ownership, technology transfer, or association of Indian scientists/institutions in R&D.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\08. Biological Diversity Act, 2002.docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme This Act is the domestic legal backbone connecting India's Patents Act (Sec. 3(p) and the biological-source disclosure requirement under Sec. 10(4)(ii)(D)), TKDL, and CBD/Nagoya Protocol obligations into one access-and-benefit-sharing (ABS) framework. Note: Source excerpt: Section 2 definitions.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\09. Biological Diversity Rules, 2024.docx
text: Purpose Procedural rules framed under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (as amended in 2023), governing the constitution and functioning of the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) and implementation of access-and-benefit-sharing (ABS) requirements.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\09. Biological Diversity Rules, 2024.docx
text: Rule 3 - Appointment of Chairperson The Chairperson of the (NBA) Authority is appointed by the Central Government. Appointment is made either on deputation, or by selection from outside government; if by deputation, the officer must not be below the rank of Additional Secretary to the Government of India.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\09. Biological Diversity Rules, 2024.docx
text: Rule 7 - Resignation/vacancy of non-official members A non-official member may resign at any time by written notice to the Central Government; the seat then becomes vacant. A casual vacancy of a non-official member is filled by fresh nomination; the newly nominated member holds office only for the remainder of the original member's term.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\09. Biological Diversity Rules, 2024.docx
text: Why this matters These governance rules keep the NBA's leadership properly staffed and senior enough (Additional Secretary-level or equivalent) to take authoritative decisions on ABS approvals, IPR clearances and biopiracy enforcement discussed under the parent 2002 Act. Note: Source excerpt: Sections/Rules 3 and 7.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\10. Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.docx
text: Purpose Regulates the import, manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs and cosmetics in India, including a dedicated regime for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani (ASU) drugs; enforced together with the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\10. Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.docx
text: Section 3 - key definitions 'Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug' includes all medicines intended for internal/external use in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease/disorder in humans or animals, and manufactured exclusively in accordance with the formulae described in the authoritative books of the respective systems specified in the First Schedule to the Act. Also includes patent or proprietary ASU medicines - i.e. formulated on scientific principles of these systems but not necessarily named in the authoritative texts.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\10. Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.docx
text: Why it matters Provides the statutory definition that anchors licensing, manufacturing standards (GMP for ASU drugs), and labelling requirements specific to traditional-medicine products, distinct from allopathic drugs. The reference to 'authoritative books' (Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Bhavaprakasha, Ashtanga Hridaya, etc. for Ayurveda) ties classical textual traditional knowledge directly into modern drug regulation. Note: Source excerpt: Section 3 definitions.

source_title: Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\11. Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954.docx
text: Section 3 - Prohibited advertisements Purpose Prohibits misleading/objectionable advertisements of drugs (including ASU drugs) and 'magic remedies' claiming miraculous or magical curative properties, to protect the public from quackery.

source_title: Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\11. Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954.docx
text: Section 3 - what is prohibited No person may take part in publishing any advertisement referring to a drug in terms that suggest or are calculated to lead to its use for: (a) procuring miscarriage in women, or preventing conception; (b) maintaining or improving capacity for sexual pleasure; (c) correcting menstrual disorders in women; and a range of similarly specified conditions listed in the Schedule to the Act (e.g. diseases for which self-medication advertising is barred).

source_title: Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\11. Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954.docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme Directly relevant to marketing of Ayurvedic/traditional formulations - claims of 'magical' or miracle cures for the scheduled conditions, even for genuinely traditional remedies, are advertising offences under this Act, reinforcing the need for scientifically substantiated claims. Note: Source excerpt: Section 3.

source_title: Food Safety and Standards (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\12. FSS (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022 - Gazette Notification.docx
text: Purpose A dedicated regulatory category created by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) for 'Ayurveda Aahara' products - traditional Ayurvedic food/dietary preparations that sit at the interface of food and Ayurvedic medicine, so they can be regulated as food rather than requiring drug licensing.

source_title: Food Safety and Standards (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\12. FSS (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022 - Gazette Notification.docx
text: Key features Defines 'Ayurveda Aahara' as a food product formulated using ingredients/formulations described in the authoritative books of Ayurveda listed under the First Schedule of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, or in the FSSAI-approved list, and prepared without therapeutic claims that would classify it as a drug. Mandates labelling with the words 'Ayurveda Aahara' along with a standard disclaimer/logo, so consumers can distinguish these products from ordinary processed foods and from licensed Ayurvedic medicines. Prohibits disease-cure or treatment claims on Ayurveda Aahara products - such claims would move the product into 'drug' territory under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act instead of 'food' under FSS law. Lays down permitted ingredients, manufacturing/hygiene standards and an approval/registration pathway through FSSAI, separate from Ayush drug licensing.

source_title: Food Safety and Standards (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\12. FSS (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022 - Gazette Notification.docx
text: Why it matters Creates regulatory clarity for the fast-growing Ayurvedic nutraceutical/functional-food industry, avoiding the earlier ambiguity of whether such products should be licensed as food or drugs, and closes a gap between the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the FSS Act, 2006. Note: Source: 8-page Gazette notification issued by FSSAI.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\13. Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL).docx
text: What it is TKDL is India's pioneering initiative to protect Indian traditional medicinal knowledge from misappropriation at international patent offices, by converting India's traditional-medicine literature into searchable, prior-art-ready form.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\13. Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL).docx
text: Why it was needed Over 70% of India's population depends on traditional medicine for healthcare, making misuse of this knowledge a livelihood/heritage issue for indigenous and local communities. Trigger case: grant of a US patent on the wound-healing properties of turmeric, later revoked only after time, effort and money were spent proving prior art existed. India's traditional-medicine literature exists in Sanskrit, Hindi, Arabic, Urdu, Tamil and other ancient/local-dialect texts inaccessible to international patent examiners - a language/format barrier TKDL was built to overcome.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\13. Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL).docx
text: How it works Systematically converts/structures textual content of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Sowa Rigpa and Yoga into five languages - English, Japanese, French, German, Spanish - using an in-house classification system called the Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification (TKRC). More than 4.54 lakh formulations/practices have been transcribed into the TKDL database. TKRC created ~200 sub-groups under IPC code A61K 36/00 (vs a handful earlier under A61K 35/00), greatly improving prior-art search quality for medicinal-plant patent applications. TKDL specifications were adopted internationally in 2003 by WIPO's Intergovernmental Committee (IGC) on IP, Genetic Resources, Traditional Knowledge and Folklore.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\13. Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL).docx
text: Access and impact TKDL access is granted (under non-disclosure agreements) to 16 patent offices, including EPO, USPTO, JPO, UKIPO, and the Indian Patent Office - examiners may use it only for search/examination, not disclose contents to third parties (except for citation purposes). Also used to file pre-grant oppositions with TKDL prior-art evidence at international patent offices. Impact: 324+ patent applications have been set aside, withdrawn or amended based on TKDL prior art at little to no cost and within weeks/months - contrasted with the ~7 crore rupees APEDA spent purely in legal fees to revoke a few claims of the Basmati rice patent.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\13. Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL).docx
text: Significance TKDL is a proactive deterrent against biopiracy: by making TK prior art visible to examiners before a wrongful patent is even granted, it avoids costly after-the-fact litigation and has set an international benchmark for TK protection in other TK-rich countries.

source_title: Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS)
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\14. TRIPS Agreement.docx
text: What it is A WTO Agreement (1994) setting minimum global standards for IP protection and enforcement, binding on all WTO member states, including India. It is the reason most Indian IP statutes (Patents, Trade Marks, Copyright, PPV&FR, GI Acts) were amended post-1995.

source_title: Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS)
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\14. TRIPS Agreement.docx
text: Article 27 - Patentable subject matter Patents must be available for any inventions - products or processes, any field of technology - provided they are new, involve an inventive step, and are industrially applicable, without discrimination based on place of invention, field of technology, or whether products are imported/locally made. Members MAY exclude from patentability inventions whose commercial exploitation must be prevented to protect public order/morality, including human/animal/plant life/health or to avoid serious environmental harm - but not merely because domestic law prohibits the exploitation. Members MAY also exclude: (a) diagnostic, therapeutic and surgical methods for treating humans or animals; (b) plants and animals (other than micro-organisms) and essentially biological processes for producing plants/animals (non-biological/microbiological processes must still be patentable) - BUT members must protect plant varieties either by patents, an effective sui generis system, or a combination (this is the TRIPS basis for India's PPV&FR Act, 2001).

source_title: Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS)
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\14. TRIPS Agreement.docx
text: Article 39 - Protection of undisclosed information Members must protect undisclosed information (trade secrets) against unfair-competition-style misuse, provided it is (a) secret, (b) has commercial value because it is secret, and (c) has been subject to reasonable steps to keep it secret. Where governments require submission of undisclosed test data as a condition for approving marketing of pharmaceutical/agrochemical products using new chemical entities, that data must be protected against unfair commercial use and, generally, against disclosure.

source_title: Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS)
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\14. TRIPS Agreement.docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme Article 27.3(b)'s plant-variety carve-out is why India built a sui generis regime instead of extending patents to plant varieties, and Article 39 underlies later debates on protecting clinical/test data for Ayurvedic/botanical drugs. Note: Source excerpt: Articles 27 and 39.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\15. Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).docx
text: What it is A multilateral treaty opened for signature at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit; the first global agreement to treat biodiversity conservation as a matter of common concern while affirming national sovereignty over genetic resources. India's Biological Diversity Act, 2002 was enacted to implement it.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\15. Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).docx
text: Article 1 - Objectives (the CBD's three pillars) Conservation of biological diversity. Sustainable use of its components. Fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising from the utilisation of genetic resources - through appropriate access to genetic resources, appropriate transfer of relevant technologies (taking into account rights over resources and technologies), and appropriate funding.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\15. Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).docx
text: Article 15 - Access to genetic resources Recognises the sovereign rights of States over their natural resources - authority to determine access rests with national governments, subject to national legislation. Parties should endeavour to facilitate access for environmentally sound uses by other parties and avoid imposing restrictions counter to the Convention's objectives. Access, where granted, must be on mutually agreed terms (MAT) and subject to the prior informed consent (PIC) of the providing party, unless that party decides otherwise. Parties must aim to share, fairly and equitably, the results of research/development and the benefits of commercial/other utilisation of genetic resources with the providing party, on mutually agreed terms.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\15. Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme The CBD's PIC + MAT + benefit-sharing framework is the template later elaborated by the Nagoya Protocol and domesticated in India through the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (NBA/SBB/BMC approval system). Note: Source excerpt: Articles 1 and 15.

source_title: Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\16. Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing.docx
text: What it is A supplementary agreement to the CBD (adopted 2010, Nagoya, Japan; in force 2014) that gives detailed, legally binding implementation rules for the CBD's Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) objective, including for traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources.

source_title: Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\16. Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing.docx
text: Article 5 - Fair and equitable benefit-sharing Benefits from utilisation of genetic resources (and subsequent applications/commercialisation) must be shared fairly with the providing/country-of-origin Party, on mutually agreed terms. Parties must legislate to ensure benefits from genetic resources held by indigenous and local communities (per domestic law) are shared fairly with those communities. Benefits may be monetary and non-monetary (per the Protocol's Annex). Benefits from use of traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources must similarly be shared fairly with the indigenous/local communities holding that knowledge, on mutually agreed terms.

source_title: Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\16. Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing.docx
text: Article 6 - Access to genetic resources Access requires the prior informed consent (PIC) of the providing/country-of-origin Party, subject to that Party's sovereign rights and domestic ABS legislation. Where indigenous/local communities have an established right to grant access, their PIC or approval/involvement must also be obtained. Parties requiring PIC must ensure: legal certainty/clarity/transparency of ABS rules; fair, non-arbitrary access procedures; published information on how to apply for PIC; timely, clear, written decisions by a competent authority; issuance of a permit as evidence of PIC/mutually agreed terms (MAT); and, where applicable, criteria for community-level PIC. MAT should be set out in writing and may cover dispute settlement, IPR-related benefit-sharing, third-party use, and change-of-intent clauses.

source_title: Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization
section_or_article: Article 7 - Access to associated traditional knowledge
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\16. Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing.docx
text: Article 7 - Access to associated traditional knowledge Traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources, held by indigenous/local communities, must be accessed only with their prior and informed consent (or approval/involvement), and only after mutually agreed terms have been established. Relevance to IP/TK theme Nagoya's PIC + MAT machinery is exactly what India's NBA/SBB/BMC system under the Biological Diversity Act operationalises domestically, and is the treaty-level ancestor of the disclosure obligations now expanded by the 2024 WIPO GRATK Treaty (see file 17). Note: Source excerpt: Articles 5, 6 and 7.

source_title: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (2024)
section_or_article: Overview - Adoption and entry into force
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\17. WIPO Treaty on IP, Genetic Resources and Traditional Knowledge (2024).docx
text: Adoption and entry into force Adopted by WIPO Member States on 24 May 2024; open for signature until 23 May 2025. Enters into force 3 months after 15 ratifications/accessions are deposited. Open to any WIPO Member State and the European Union; other IGOs may join on Assembly decision.

source_title: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (2024)
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\17. WIPO Treaty on IP, Genetic Resources and Traditional Knowledge (2024).docx
text: Objectives To enhance the efficacy, transparency and quality of the patent system with respect to genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge (associated TK), and to prevent erroneous grant of patents for inventions that are not novel/inventive over genetic resources and associated TK.

source_title: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (2024)
section_or_article: Overview - Mandatory patent disclosure requirement (core obligation)
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\17. WIPO Treaty on IP, Genetic Resources and Traditional Knowledge (2024).docx
text: Mandatory patent disclosure requirement (core obligation) Where a claimed invention is 'based on' genetic resources and/or associated TK, patent applicants must disclose the country of origin of the genetic resources, and/or the indigenous peoples/local community providing the associated TK. If that is unknown, the source must be disclosed instead; if neither is known, the applicant must declare so. Patent offices must provide guidance but have no obligation to verify the authenticity of the disclosure. Sanctions, remedies and safeguards Failure to disclose is subject to appropriate, effective and proportionate measures; applicants get a chance to rectify a failure unless there is fraudulent conduct/intent. Post-grant sanctions apply only where there was fraudulent intent. Crucially: absent fraud, a patent cannot be revoked, invalidated or rendered unenforceable solely for failure to disclose - a major safeguard for patentees.

source_title: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (2024)
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\17. WIPO Treaty on IP, Genetic Resources and Traditional Knowledge (2024).docx
text: Other key features Non-retroactivity: no Treaty obligation applies to patent applications filed before the Treaty enters into force. Information systems: encourages databases of genetic resources/associated TK (developed with Indigenous Peoples/local communities where relevant) accessible to patent offices for search and examination - conceptually similar to India's TKDL. Review mechanism: built-in review 4 years after entry into force, including possible extension of the disclosure requirement to other IP forms, to derivatives, and to new/emerging technologies. No reservations to the Treaty are permitted; Parties are free to choose their own method of domestic implementation.

source_title: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (2024)
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\17. WIPO Treaty on IP, Genetic Resources and Traditional Knowledge (2024).docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme This is the newest and highest-level international instrument in the whole TK-protection chain (CBD → Nagoya Protocol → domestic ABS laws → this Treaty), making patent-level source disclosure a binding international norm rather than just a national-law practice (as already exists, in a stronger form, under India's Patents Act Sec. 10(4)). Note: Source: official WIPO summary of the Treaty.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\18. Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT).docx
text: What it is A WIPO-administered treaty enabling applicants to seek patent protection for an invention simultaneously in a large number of countries by filing a single 'international' patent application, instead of filing separate national applications from the outset. It does NOT grant an international patent - grant remains a national/regional matter.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\18. Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT).docx
text: International phase Filing: applicant files one international application with a Receiving Office (national IP office or WIPO's International Bureau), designating (automatically, all) PCT contracting states. International search: an International Searching Authority (ISA) issues an International Search Report (ISR) and a Written Opinion on patentability. International publication: the application is published (with the ISR) 18 months after the priority date. Optional Chapter II - International Preliminary Examination: applicant may request a more detailed preliminary opinion from an International Preliminary Examining Authority (IPEA).

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\18. Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT).docx
text: National phase Applicant must enter the 'national phase' before each patent office where protection is desired, generally within 30/31 months from the priority date - filing translations, paying national fees, and appointing local agents as required. Each designated national/regional office then examines and grants (or refuses) a patent under its own domestic law - the PCT streamlines filing/search but each country still decides patentability independently.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\18. Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT).docx
text: Key advantages Delays the (expensive) national-phase costs by up to 18 months compared to direct Paris Convention filing (12-month priority window). Centralised search/examination reduces duplicated effort and gives applicants an early view of patentability before committing to costly multi-country filings. Single, uniform filing format accepted by all contracting states' offices.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\18. Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT).docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme PCT applications for inventions based on genetic resources/traditional knowledge (e.g. botanical-drug patents) increasingly need to satisfy source-disclosure requirements at the national-phase stage in countries like India, even though the PCT itself is procedurally neutral on substantive patentability standards such as Sec. 3(p). Note: Source: full treaty text (WIPO).

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\19. Madrid System - International Registration of Marks.docx
text: What it is A WIPO-administered system allowing the owner of a trademark to obtain protection in multiple member countries/regions by filing a single international application, in one language, with one set of fees, through their national/regional trademark office (the 'Office of origin'). How it works (Chapter II - users' perspective) Basic requirement: applicant must already have a 'basic mark' - a pending application or existing registration - in their home ('Office of origin') trademark office. Filing: the international application is filed through the Office of origin, which certifies that the international application corresponds to the basic mark, then forwards it to WIPO's International Bureau. International registration: WIPO records the mark in the International Register and publishes it in the WIPO Gazette of International Marks; it then notifies each designated contracting party (country/region chosen for protection). National examination: each designated office examines the mark under its own domestic law and may refuse protection within a set time limit (12 or 18 months) - if no refusal is issued, the mark is protected there as if directly registered. Term: an international registration is valid for 10 years, renewable indefinitely for further 10-year periods, directly at WIPO (no need to renew separately in each country). Dependency ('central attack'): for the first 5 years, the international registration remains dependent on the basic mark - if the basic mark is cancelled/refused/withdrawn, the international registration falls with it (though it can be 'transformed' into national applications in each designated country, retaining the original filing date). Subsequent designation: protection can be extended to further contracting parties after the initial registration, without refiling the whole application.

section_or_article: Chapter I: Introduction - general overview, advantages of the Madrid System.
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\19. Madrid System - International Registration of Marks.docx
text: Chapter I: Introduction - general overview, advantages of the Madrid System. Chapter II: The Madrid System from the users' perspective - the practical filing/registration/renewal procedure (summarised above). Chapter III: Guide for Offices of members of the Madrid System - procedural guide for national IP offices administering incoming/outgoing Madrid applications.

section_or_article: Chapter IV: Becoming a member of the Protocol.
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\19. Madrid System - International Registration of Marks.docx
text: Chapter IV: Becoming a member of the Protocol. Relevance Directly analogous to the PCT but for trademarks - relevant for Ayurvedic/herbal brands seeking cost-effective multi-country trademark protection alongside GI and patent strategies. Note: Source: WIPO Guide to the Madrid System (270 pages) - overview of Chapters I-IV.

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\20. Hague System - International Registration of Designs.docx
text: What it is A WIPO-administered system, analogous to the Madrid System for trademarks and the PCT for patents, that allows an applicant to protect an industrial design in multiple countries/regions through a single international application filed directly with WIPO's International Bureau (or via an eligible national/regional office).

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\20. Hague System - International Registration of Designs.docx
text: How it works Unlike Madrid, the Hague System does not require a prior 'basic' national design registration/application - an applicant can file the international application directly. A single international application can include multiple designs (up to 100, subject to a same-class rule), each designating one or more of the contracting parties where protection is sought. International registration: WIPO records the design in the International Register and publishes it in the International Designs Bulletin (immediately or after a permissible deferment of publication). Each designated contracting party then examines (if it has a substantive-examination system) and may refuse protection within a prescribed time limit (6 or 12 months); absent refusal, the design is protected as if registered directly there. Term: initial 5-year term, renewable in blocks of 5 years, up to the maximum term allowed under each designated party's domestic law (subject to a Hague Agreement ceiling).

source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\20. Hague System - International Registration of Designs.docx
text: Chapter VI: Changes and renewals. Chapter VII: London Act (1934) and Hague Act (1960) - legacy Acts of the Agreement, largely superseded by the 1999 Geneva Act now in common use. Relevance India is not yet a member of the Hague Agreement (as of this guide's date), but the system is studied comparatively alongside India's own Designs Act, 2000 (file 05) as the international counterpart for industrial-design filing strategy. Note: Source: WIPO Guide to the Hague System (102 pages) - overview of Chapters I-VII.

source_title: Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\21. Budapest Treaty on Deposit of Microorganisms.docx
text: Why it exists Patent law requires an invention to be disclosed (usually in writing) so a person skilled in the art can reproduce it. Where the invention involves a micro-organism (or other biological material), a written description alone cannot fully disclose it - only a deposited physical sample can. Before this Treaty, applicants had to separately deposit the same micro-organism in every country where they sought a patent.

source_title: Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\21. Budapest Treaty on Deposit of Microorganisms.docx
text: Main feature A single deposit of a micro-organism with any 'International Depositary Authority' (IDA) suffices for patent procedure before ALL contracting states' national offices, and before any regional patent office that has declared it recognises the Treaty (e.g. EPO, EAPO, OAPI, ARIPO) - eliminating the need to deposit separately in every country of filing.

source_title: Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\21. Budapest Treaty on Deposit of Microorganisms.docx
text: International Depositary Authorities (IDAs) An IDA is typically a scientific 'culture collection' institution capable of storing micro-organisms; it becomes an IDA once its host contracting state furnishes assurances to the WIPO Director General that it meets and will continue to meet the Treaty's requirements. As of the source date there were 53 IDAs worldwide, including several in India, the UK, the Republic of Korea, China, Italy, Poland, Russia and the USA. 'Micro-organism' is interpreted broadly to cover any biological material whose deposit is necessary for disclosure - especially relevant to food and pharmaceutical inventions.

source_title: Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\21. Budapest Treaty on Deposit of Microorganisms.docx
text: Benefits to applicants Cost saving: one deposit with one IDA instead of repeated deposits in every filing country. Security: a uniform system of deposit, recognition and sample-furnishing across all contracting states.

source_title: Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\21. Budapest Treaty on Deposit of Microorganisms.docx
text: Administration Creates a Budapest Union and Assembly (member states); no budget/financial contributions are required from member states, and no state is required to establish an IDA. Open to States party to the Paris Convention (1883); instruments of ratification/accession are deposited with the WIPO Director General.

source_title: Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\21. Budapest Treaty on Deposit of Microorganisms.docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme Directly relevant to biotechnology and botanical-drug patents (see files 22) where a strain, culture or seed sample must be deposited to satisfy enablement/disclosure requirements. Note: Source: WIPO general description of the Treaty.

source_title: Botanical Drug Development - Guidance for Industry
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\22a. FDA Guidance - Botanical Drug Development.docx
text: What it is US FDA guidance (non-binding, but reflects current FDA thinking) on developing botanical products - including traditional/herbal remedies - into approved prescription or OTC 'botanical drugs', through the standard IND (Investigational New Drug) and NDA (New Drug Application) pathway.

source_title: Botanical Drug Development - Guidance for Industry
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\22a. FDA Guidance - Botanical Drug Development.docx
text: Key concepts 'Botanical drug': a drug product derived from plant materials, algae, macroscopic fungi or combinations - can range from crude, minimally processed plant material to more purified/characterized botanical drug substances. Recognises that botanical drugs are often chemically complex mixtures (unlike single-molecule synthetic drugs), so full chemical characterisation of every constituent is not always required before clinical development, provided quality/consistency is controlled. Allows a reduced non-clinical (toxicology) data package for Phase 1/2 trials where there is a documented history of prior human use of the botanical (e.g. traditional/marketed use), subject to safety caveats. Chemistry, Manufacturing & Controls (CMC) emphasis: because botanicals are complex mixtures, consistent raw-material sourcing/identification (botanical/geographic/harvest specifications), process controls, and batch-to-batch consistency testing (e.g. chromatographic fingerprinting) become central to quality assurance instead of relying solely on single-molecule potency assays. The same rigorous efficacy/safety evidentiary standard (adequate, well-controlled clinical trials) applies for final marketing approval as for any other drug - the relaxed early-stage requirements are a development-pathway accommodation, not a lower approval bar.

source_title: Botanical Drug Development - Guidance for Industry
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\22a. FDA Guidance - Botanical Drug Development.docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme Provides the US regulatory template that Ayurvedic/herbal drug developers must navigate to move traditional formulations into the US pharmaceutical market - directly parallel to India's own ASU drug licensing under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act (file 10) and to the EMA's herbal guideline (file 22b). Note: Source: FDA guidance document (34 pages) - key themes.

source_title: Guideline on Declaration of Herbal Substances and Herbal Preparations in Herbal Medicinal Products / Traditional Herbal Medicinal Products
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\22b. EMA Guideline - Herbal Substances and Preparations.docx
text: What it is A European regulatory guideline (developed by EMA's Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products - HMPC - together with the human and veterinary medicines committees) specifying how herbal substances and herbal preparations must be named/declared on labelling and in product information for both full 'herbal medicinal products' and simplified-registration 'traditional herbal medicinal products' in the EU.

source_title: Guideline on Declaration of Herbal Substances and Herbal Preparations in Herbal Medicinal Products / Traditional Herbal Medicinal Products
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\22b. EMA Guideline - Herbal Substances and Preparations.docx
text: Key concepts Distinguishes 'herbal substance' (the plant material itself - whole, fragmented or cut plants, algae, fungi, lichen, usually unprocessed and typically dried) from 'herbal preparation' (the product obtained by subjecting herbal substances to processes such as extraction, distillation, expression, fractionation, purification, concentration or fermentation). Requires declaration to specify the botanical/scientific (Latin binomial) name of the source plant, the plant part used, and (for preparations) the type of preparation and the extraction/solvent ratio (e.g. drug-extract ratio, DER). Aims for consistent, unambiguous naming across EU member states so that consumers, prescribers and regulators can identify exactly which herbal material and processing method is in a given product - important because different plant parts/extraction methods can have very different pharmacological profiles even from the 'same' plant.

source_title: Guideline on Declaration of Herbal Substances and Herbal Preparations in Herbal Medicinal Products / Traditional Herbal Medicinal Products
source_file: C:\Users\sharm\Downloads\sih2026045\Corpus Research\My Notes\22b. EMA Guideline - Herbal Substances and Preparations.docx
text: Relevance to IP/TK theme Precise botanical/preparation declaration is the EU counterpart to the FDA's CMC/quality-control emphasis (file 22a) and is essential groundwork for any Indian Ayurvedic/herbal exporter seeking 'traditional herbal medicinal product' registration in the EU - and reinforces, from a different angle, why accurate source/species identification matters for both regulatory approval and TK-related patent disclosure obligations (files 08, 17). Note: Source: EMA guideline document (21 pages) - key themes.
